poems: 8:00. Somewhere a man in a Corolla is merging on faith alone.

Open the inbox.
Close it.
Open it again.
It is a refrigerator and you are still not hungry.
A school bus stop arm swings out. The red octagon shakes a little and holds.
Somewhere it is three minutes into the workday and someone has already replied all.
The bagel is toasting. This will be the last uncontested decision of the day.

Things in the door pocket:
a parking receipt,
one glove,
three straw wrappers,
an ice scraper,
a nickel.

8:06. The revolving door meters the building's intake,
four at a time.

8:07. A travel mug forgotten on a car roof
rides four blocks, a legend in the making.
8:08, and the drop-off lane moves the way a glacier moves.
Your badge is in the other coat. It has always been in the other coat.
Overheard in the stairwell: "She knows. She just doesn't know know."
A paper cup lid on the roof of a Camry, still there at the light, still there after.

8:12. The on-ramp performs its zipper merge,
one grudge at a time.
The dog's day already peaked.
Merge, v. To insist politely at forty miles an hour.
8:15. The kitchen after the first wave: crumbs, a knife standing up in the peanut butter, one shoe.
Two lanes become one lane and everyone believes they were here first.

You are not late yet.
You are in the part of the morning where that is still true.

A tie knotted on the train,
no mirror, third try.
Parking lot. Engine off, radio still on.
8:20. Somewhere they are calling zone four. The overhead bins are already a rumor.

The date goes on the whiteboard,
underlined by someone who loves the marker.
Push the button twice. It does nothing twice.

8:23. Somebody staples four pages
with the authority of a judge.
Your headphones are in and nothing is playing. Nobody needs to know that.
A stroller wheel wedged in a sidewalk crack. A thumb on the brake.
Somewhere it is 8:26 in the evening and the same person is finally sitting down.

Reasons offered at the front desk:
traffic,
the bridge,
the dog,
the tunnel,
the truth.
The bus kneels. The whole thing sighs down two inches for one man with a cane.
A minute before anything starts, everyone is fine.
8:30. Half the county is in a car and the other half is about to be.
The woman at the daycare gate knows your kid's name and not yours. Fair enough.

8:32. A bus shelter ad for an injury lawyer,
smiling through scratched glass.
The cuff inflates. The nurse looks at the ceiling and counts.

MEDIUM DRIP
NO ROOM
name spelled wrong again
$2.85
Everyone in this elevator has agreed to look at the same corner of the ceiling.
Somebody is already eating their lunch.

Start with the hard one, you said.
Here is the hard one.
A man in a reflective vest waves a truck backward with two fingers, unhurried.
Nothing has gone wrong yet that anyone could have prevented.
The framers are two hours in already, radio propped on a sawhorse.
A kettle clicks off. Nobody here is dressed.
8:42. Optimism peaks. It will not be reported.
A school bus, empty now, taking the corner faster than it did full.
In the lost and found by now: a retainer, a trumpet, four jackets, one sock.
Fifteen minutes is enough to do one thing or to think about doing three.
The train doors close on a backpack strap and open again.
8:47. A shift change is finally over and the coffee tastes like the machine it came from.

Take the stairs.
Sign the sheet.
Nod at the guard who has seen everything.
The parking garage takes your money without comment.

8:50. Every radio in the parking garage
arrives mid-chorus of the same song.
A rubber band around the mail on a stoop.
Two hard hats, one thermos, no words.

8:53. Old magazines fanned with care
for no one.
In the break room, somebody's yogurt has a name on it in permanent marker, written twice.
Five to nine. The last of the good parking.
A woman jogs the last thirty yards to the corner, then walks, having won.
The intercom crackles once, thinks better of it.
8:58. Two minutes left that belong to nobody.
The last minute of the hour goes to finding a pen that works.
